transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (CISO, Keystone Bank), Marcus Vale (Cloud Architect), Priya Singh (Compliance Manager)

Summary (auto-generated, brief):
Redwood overview of audit logging and admin activity capture. Discussion focused on what events are captured (admin actions, login attempts, API keys, model usage), export options (S3, webhook, SIEM connectors), retention and custom retention windows, encryption/KMS usage on exported logs, and request for sample schema and SOC2/ISO artifacts. Next steps agreed.

Transcript:
00:00 Jenna: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
00:04 Laura: yes we can, thanks. we wanted to go through audit logs and admin activity specifically — what you capture, how we can export, retention, encryption.
00:12 Jenna: great, that's Omar and I will run through most of the logging details. Omar are you on?
00:17 Omar: yeah hi all, Omar Patel, Redwood infra SE. i'll jump in on schema and export questions.
00:22 Marcus: quick context — we're Keystone cloud team evaluating private deployment vs dedicated. compliance needs drive our logging requirements.
00:28 Priya: and from compliance we need a clear retention policy, proof of immutability for some records, and a way to pull logs into our SIEM.
00:34 Omar: totally makes sense. high level — Redwood collects two major classes of logs: platform audit logs (admin activity, auth events, role/permission changes, API key events) and request-level logs (requests to the inference API, model and route metadata, token counts).
00:50 Laura: request-level logs — do those include full user prompt text? that's sensitive for us.
00:55 Omar: good question. by default we capture request metadata and headers, request IDs, route name, model id, response status, token counts. full prompt text is not stored in audit logs by default on hosted tiers. for customers on Private/Dedicated deployments you can enable request logging but we support field-level redaction and masking; we can redact PII and sensitive prompt content before writing to the audit stream.
01:18 Marcus: so for hosted, no prompt text in audit logs — okay. if we enable exports to S3, what's included?
01:24 Omar: export payloads can be customized. default export includes timestamp, actor (user id or service principal), event type (e.g., admin.create_user, api.request, api.key.rotate), resource id, route/model, status, duration, and token usage. If you opt-in for request bodies, those are in a separate field and we can apply redaction rules. We provide both JSON and newline-delimited JSON (ndjson) formats; CSV for summary exports.
01:49 Priya: immutability — we need tamper-evidence. can logs be write-once?
01:54 Omar: we support export to customer-owned S3 with bucket policies and object-lock enabled. for Private deployments, you control the storage and can enable S3 Object Lock/Governance mode. additionally our audit logs include an append-only sequence number and hash chain in metadata to detect tampering — it's in the schema and we can show how to validate.
02:16 Laura: do you have sample schema? we'd like to run it through our parsers.
02:20 Jenna: Omar will share the schema after the call.
02:23 Omar: yes i'll drop a sample ndjson with event samples (admin.user.create, admin.role.update, auth.login.failure, api.key.create, api.key.revoke, model.deploy, export.started/export.completed).
02:36 Marcus: what about real-time streaming into our SIEM? we use Splunk and Datadog.
02:40 Omar: we have two main real-time paths: (1) push via HTTPS webhook to your collector (with retries and backoff), (2) direct connector for S3 -> SIEM ingestion, and (3) for Splunk we have a HEC-compatible endpoint example. For Datadog you can forward via webhook or through our CloudTrail-compatible export if using AWS.
03:05 Priya: retention ranges — what are the options? we may need 1 year for some admin activity and 7 years for select audit trails per policy.
03:12 Omar: on Hosted we offer retention tiers: 30 days default, 90 days, 1 year, and custom by contract for enterprise (we can do 7 years via archive to customer S3). For Dedicated/Private you manage retention — Redwood will retain on the control plane per your config, and long-term archive goes to customer-owned buckets. Keep in mind cost/latency tradeoffs for longer retention.
03:34 Laura: export security — are exported logs encrypted with our KMS?
03:38 Omar: yes, when shipping to customer S3, you can specify your KMS key (customer-managed CMKs). For hosted exports to Redwood-managed buckets we use server-side encryption with keys managed by Redwood, but we also offer envelope encryption with customer KMS for extra control.
03:55 Marcus: what about access controls for who can view logs in the console? RBAC?
04:00 Omar: RBAC in Redwood Console supports role-based permissions. Audit log viewing is controlled by the role 'logs.viewer' or 'admin'. We integrate with SSO (SAML/Okta, Azure AD). All console access events themselves are logged.
04:12 Priya: do you capture admin console actions like policy changes, role grants, and KMS changes?
04:16 Omar: yes those are part of admin activity events. event types include admin.policy.update, admin.kms.key.rotate, admin.role.grant, admin.role.revoke, etc. each event captures actor, timestamp, target resource, prior_state and new_state diffs where applicable. (note: transcript may show 'prior_state' as 'pryor state' in the raw export sometimes).
04:40 Laura: governance — we need signed logs for certain workflows. you mentioned a hash chain earlier, can you expand?
04:45 Omar: the schema includes an optional signature block. when enabled, each batch of exported events includes a cryptographic hash and signature using Redwood's private signing key; if you prefer, we can sign with an ephemeral key you provide via KMS. That way you can verify integrity against signatures and detect rewrites.
05:05 Marcus: latency — if we stream logs to our SIEM, what's expected delay?
05:09 Omar: typical push latency is under 5 seconds for webhook delivery; with retries it may stretch. For S3 batch exports, we support near-real-time (1-2 min window) or scheduled hourly/daily exports.
05:21 Laura: PII removal — is there an automated redaction or a rules engine?
05:25 Omar: we have a rules engine. you define patterns and fields to redact; we also provide prebuilt PII patterns (emails, SSNs, credit card patterns). For Private, you can run the engine locally before export to ensure no sensitive text leaves your VPC.
05:40 Jenna: quick note — SOC 2 and ISO docs are in the compliance pack i'll attach after the call.
05:45 Priya: can you confirm which events are included for API keys? we need full lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, failed uses).
05:51 Omar: yes full lifecycle: api.key.create, api.key.rotate, api.key.disable, api.key.revoke, auth.token.failed, auth.token.success, plus metadata like IP, user-agent, request origin.
06:06 Marcus: anything captured about model artifacts? e.g., model uploads or deploys and who triggered them.
06:10 Omar: model.deploy, model.upload, model.version.rollback, and model.quantize were specifically called out; they capture actor, model hash/id, environment, and config. This is useful for forensic audits.
06:26 Laura: retention for request-level logs where prompts are opt-in — do you recommend always redacting before sending to S3?
06:32 Omar: from a best-practice perspective, redact in-platform before sending to external storage unless the customer-managed KMS and bucket policies meet your data residency and access controls. Many banks prefer redact + store only meta and a hashed pointer to full content if needed.
06:49 Priya: regarding data residency — if we run in EU region, will logs ever leave region?
06:54 Omar: no, we can pin region. for Hosted Redwood we support region-specific control planes and storage; Dedicated/Private are deployed in your VPC/region so logs stay on-prem or in your cloud region per contract.
07:06 Marcus: for compliance we need a sample pipeline to ingest logs into Splunk with field mappings.
07:11 Omar: i'll include a Splunk HEC example and a mapping file. the mapping shows field names we emit: event_time, actor_id, actor_email, event_type, resource_id, resource_type, prev_state, new_state, request_id, token_count, model_id, region, signature_hash.
07:33 Jenna: there's sometimes imperfect transcription — we posted a note in the deck about that — but main point is schema will be shared.
07:38 Marcus: any limits on retention size or egress rates?
07:42 Omar: Hosted tiers have per-account ingestion limits by plan; for high-volume customers we recommend Dedicated and direct S3 export to avoid rate constraints. We can set up dedicated ingestion pipelines for large customers.
07:56 Laura: legal — if there's an incident and auditors request logs, what's the turnaround?
08:00 Omar: we support on-demand exports and we can provide forensically-signed bundles. turnaround depends on retention policy and whether logs are archived; typical SLA for signed bundle requests is 48-72 hours for standard contracts, faster for enterprise support.
08:16 Priya: do you maintain a separate admin audit stream for changes to the audit config itself? we need an immutable record of who changed retention and export destinations.
08:24 Omar: yes we log changes to auditing configuration as admin.audit.config.update events (who made the change, prior config, new config). we also recommend enabling alerts for those events.
08:36 Marcus: on the topic of keys — how does key rotation look when using customer KMS? if we rotate CMK, do you re-encrypt historical exports?
08:43 Omar: historical objects remain encrypted with the key used at write time. S3 object re-encryption is managed by S3 lifecycle/replication rules if you choose to re-encrypt; Redwood does not re-encrypt historic objects by default. If you need that, we can advise on a rotation plan and re-encrypt toolchain.
09:00 Laura: auditing of Redwood personnel access — do you log support access?
09:05 Omar: yes, any support session that requires Redwood engineer access to your tenant is logged as support.session.start/support.session.end, with justification, list of resources accessed, and a temporary ephemeral access token. Those events are included in audit exports.
09:18 Priya: for PCI/finance regs we sometimes need redaction certs — can Redwood provide attestations that certain fields were redacted?
09:25 Omar: we can provide a redaction report with hashing to show original fields were redacted and provide the redaction ruleset used. For enterprise contracts we include that in the compliance pack.
09:37 Jenna: quick recap before we move to next steps — Omar will send schema + Splunk mapping and sample payloads, i'll share SOC 2/ISO artifacts, Keystone will confirm retention windows and network policy. Schedule a demo for the connectors. Does that capture it?
09:52 Laura: yep that works.
09:54 Marcus: yes thanks.
09:56 Priya: thanks everyone.
10:00 Jenna: thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and next steps.

End of transcript.
